Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

item.title: Functional Programming with Hypergraph Transformation
item.description: Complex data structures are difficult to manipulate declaratively while preserving their shape invariants. Functional languages offer pattern matching and strong static guarantees, but their type systems primarily describe tree-shaped data. Graph transformation languages support richer structures, yet their state-oriented models do not integrate naturally with value- and function-based programming. This dissertation introduces $λ_{GT}$, a functional language that integrates port-hypergraph transformation. It represents complex data as port hypergraphs, manipulates them by pattern matching, and uses types to specify global shape invariants. We formalise HyperLMNtal as a term-based graph transformation formalism, then define the syntax and call-by-value semantics of untyped $λ_{GT}$ and implement a prototype interpreter. We develop a core type system for $λ_{GT}$, prove its soundness, and relate it to graph-grammar-based typing. We extend the system with linear implication types to describe incomplete graphs arising during pattern matching. The extended system is sound with dynamic pattern-matching checks and is conservative over complete graph types. We also identify a statically safe fragment in which these checks can be eliminated. Finally, we mechanise the definitions and meta-theory in Isabelle/HOL.

item.title: Co-DRIS: Physics-Informed Predictive Belief and Variable-Impedance Learning for Reactive Catching under Coupled Uncertainty
item.description: Reactive robotic manipulation is acutely sensitive to simultaneous sensing noise, measurement dropouts, joint execution errors, and contact parameter variations. While single-frame frameworks like Domain-Randomized Instance Set (DRIS) achieve strong robustness under isolated uncertainties (86.4%), they degrade severely when perception and actuation uncertainties co-occur (27.6% across 10 coupled stress scenarios) due to memoryless encoding and fixed high-stiffness PD control. We propose Co-DRIS + SuperMimic, a perception-action co-design framework coupling: (i) an inertial world-frame physics-informed world model combining exact ballistic kinematics with a zero-initialized contact residual to roll forward missing observations and accelerate training via zero-cost counterfactual dropout consistency; (ii) an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder resolving the denoising-vs-lag deadlock; and (iii) phase-aware variable-impedance soft-catching that transitions the 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm into an overdamped regime (zeta/zeta0 ~ 2.26x) at the torque layer. Under unbiased 3-seed tail evaluation on unseen throws (15,360 throws/scenario), our method achieves 89.6 +/- 0.4% on standard benchmarks (+10.5% on 4-sigma noise to 70.5%) and 66.6 +/- 0.5% across 10 coupled/dropout stress scenarios (+39.0% over DRIS; +30.4% on 50% dropout). We further validate impedance decoupling, causal contact triggering under +0.65 s flight-time shifts, and cross-task transfer to steel-plate ping-pong bouncing (87.5% to 100.0%) and FR3+Hand catching (+8.4% under 4x noise with 6-13% lower peak impact force).

item.title: VG-GP: Uncertainty-Gated Visuo-Geometric Memory for Negative-Transfer-Resistant Grasp Adaptation
item.description: Pretrained antipodal grasping networks generalize well to canonical shapes but frequently fail zero-shot on novel objects with irregular mass distributions, thin rims, or unfamiliar handles. While episodic experience memory adapts a frozen base policy without retraining, naive retrieval suffers from visual appearance bias, negative transfer from overriding working base grasps, and degenerate closed-loop acquisition. We present VG-GP, a plug-and-play Visuo-Geometric Gaussian Process memory framework for closed-loop $SE(2)$ residual grasp transfer. First, we fuse color-invariant surface-normal DINOv2 features, canonical $SE(2)$ gripper-aligned 3D local heightmaps, and contact-geometry descriptors under a product kernel with Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) lengthscales learned strictly on source objects. Second, we model the joint posterior over the base grasp and candidate $SE(2)$ alternatives, overriding the base policy only when the joint-covariance Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) clears a risk-sensitive threshold. Third, an online counterfactual curation gate using single-record necessity and sufficiency interventions quarantines source experiences causing negative transfer. Fourth, we close the acquisition loop via Bayesian Expected Improvement (EI) over equal-budget $SE(2)$ probes. Across 42 disjoint YCB objects in ManiSkill3 (20 source, 12 development, 10 held-out test), VG-GP wraps a pretrained GR-ConvNet base policy and raises physical lift rate across all 22 unseen objects from 38.6% (34/88) to 53.4% (47/88) with zero regressions (+13 rescues, 0 losses; object-clustered 95% CI [+6.8%, +22.7%], exact McNemar $p = 0.00024$). On the 10 held-out objects, EI active acquisition reaches 45.0% (18/40 vs. 32.5% base, 5/7 of oracle headroom), achieves 55.0% probe divergence over passive fallback, and monotonically reduces epistemic uncertainty.

item.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
item.description: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

item.title: Defining the mathematical family tree with a minimal programming language
item.description: I introduce MLISP, a Turing-complete language with nine single-character commands (a b c d f 0 i j k), and use it to define 88 mathematical structures and a family tree of 65 theories that they model, with three aims: Pedagogy: It presents the mathematical structures in a unified way, with standardized presentation tableaus that define them and axiomatized theories that describe them. Connections: It highlights how they are related in the family tree via added symbols, axioms, etc. While the full tree is obviously infinite, its lower parts naturally separate into six main branches: the relational branch, the algebraic branch, the logic branch, the number branch, the set branch and the continuum branch. Foundations: The definitions, key theorems and models of each entry are verified in Lean. Mathematical structures are defined as equivalence classes of presentations, which in a constructivist spirit are defined in a simple, explicit and self-contained way in standardized presentation tableaus with minimal human baggage. For finite structures, the generating functions are defined by lookup tables. For countably infinite ones, they are instead defined computationally using MLISP, since more complex languages such as Lean are massive overkill for rigorously defining standard arithmetic operations (for example, the program "jibjbfid" defines subtraction). An interactive version is available at https://tegmark.org/mathtree. The Lean code is public, also verifies the correctness of MLISP and includes 43% of the theorems from Mathlib 2026-10-11. \end{abstract}

item.title: Solving (Vertex-Weighted) Directed Multiway Cut Faster Than $2^n$
item.description: In the Directed Multiway Cut problem, we are given a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ and a subset $T\subseteq V$, called the terminal set. The aim is to find a minimum-cardinality set $S\subseteq V\setminus T$, such that after deleting $S$, no directed path exists from one terminal to another terminal in the remaining graph. It had been an open question whether \textsc{Directed Multiway Cut} can be solved faster than the trivial running-time bound $O^*(2^{|V|})$. In this paper, we provide a positive answer to this question, presenting an algorithm with a running-time bound $O(1.9967^{|V|})$. The algorithm can also be modified to solve the weighted version (each vertex having a positive weight) in $O^*(1.9985^{|V|})$ time.

item.title: An Order-Optimal Square-Root Bound for Online Maximin Share Allocation with Known Types
item.description: An allocator knows the indivisible goods, the number $n$ of agents, and the $k$ possible additive valuations. Each agent reveals their type on arrival and must immediately receive an irrevocable bundle. Kulkarni, Mehta, and Shahkar established a deterministic guarantee of $1/k$ of maximin share (MMS) and an upper bound of $2/(\sqrt{k}-2)$ for $k>4$. We determine the optimal order $Θ(k^{-1/2})$ by constructing a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, Single-or-Select. On every arrival sequence, it gives each agent a fraction $(1/\sqrt{2}-o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ of their truncated proportional share. This share dominates MMS and is the largest target $y$ for which the item values capped at $y$ sum to at least $ny$. By specializing the construction of Kulkarni et al. to two arrivals and counting its types exactly, we sharpen the upper bound to $(\sqrt{2}+o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ even for binary valuations. For two arrivals with binary valuations and every $k\ge2$, the optimal fraction is $1/p$, where $p$ is the largest integer with $1+\binom{2p}{2}\le k$. In particular, up to six binary types permit full maximin share. For two arbitrary additive types, a different polynomial-time algorithm guarantees $4/7$ of maximin share for any number of agents. This ratio is tight for the algorithm. With three arrivals and two types, the optimal deterministic fraction is exactly $9/10$. For randomized policies with $k$ known additive types, the optimal MMS fraction guaranteed to all agents with probability at least $1-δ$ on every fixed arrival sequence is $Θ(\max\{k^{-1/2},\sqrtδ\})$ for $0\leδ<1$.

item.title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview
item.description: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.

item.title: CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence
item.description: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. On a unanimous vote, the minimum-expected-loss rule reduces calibration to one loss-derived threshold, so for two of six model configurations a gate on the vote alone never executed a clear instruction, costing 0.49 per item on TRUST-NAV against CATWAY's 0.13 and 0.09; the fused estimate avoided this on every set.

item.title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative
item.description: ERCOT publishes every generator's hourly offer curve 60 days after the operating day. Market monitors, researchers and traders use these records to study the merit order and check for withholding. PJM publishes the same kind of data with unit names replaced by codes, on the view that masking keeps offers confidential. We test that view on ERCOT data from 2024 to 2026, where names are public and so provide ground truth, by masking the records under PJM's published rules. Public EIA and EPA data match 25% of the masked units we can score (32% of their capacity) to their plant, and 45% fall within the top five guesses. PJM's feed carries the same fields, so we expect masking to fail there too. Publishing exact fuel-group totals instead does not help. An attacker who knows the other units in a group recovers one unit's high-price offers exactly, and an outsider who knows only the target's outage dates reaches a correlation of 0.77, most of it from a few renewable and hydro units that offer at very high prices (0.32 over fossil units). We propose a differentially private release: monthly totals by fuel group and price bin, with Gaussian noise calibrated under zero-concentrated differential privacy so that each unit's whole year of offers is protected. It publishes an unbiased noisy layer and derives a monotone supply curve and shares from it at no extra privacy cost. At $\varepsilon=10$ per unit-year the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth, the implied clearing price within \$3.0/MWh, and the attacker's correlation falls to 0.23. Whether an analysis still works depends on one ratio, how much the true quantity varies month to month against the noise, which predicts the accuracy of totals to within 0.05. The clearing price, supply slope and combined-cycle capacity remain usable, but no monthly release, private or exact, can answer questions about single hours or single units.

item.title: Curvature-Equilibrated Policy Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.

item.title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
item.description: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.

item.title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
item.description: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.

item.title: Stranded Compute in AI Inference Workloads: Recovering Value Through Demand Aggregation
item.description: AI inference infrastructure is commonly analyzed as an energy business. Under full total cost accounting it is not: in the reference deployment modeled here, capital recovery is 87.3% of fully loaded cost per token and electricity 3.7%. Because capital accrues per unit time irrespective of use, accelerator value is destroyed by non-utilization rather than by consumption. Yet, SLO qualified goodput reaches only 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and the decomposition of the loss chain shows that 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points arise from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve. Both are properties of a tenant's demand portfolio rather than of its silicon, and neither is diversifiable by a single tenant acting alone. Modelling reserve and idle capacity as diversifiable risk, pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants (rho = 0.3) recovers 7.3 pp of goodput, approximately $0.75M per annum per megawatt of IT capacity, or between 2.8x and 4.9x the entire annual interconnection spend of the deployment that produced it. The implication for neutral colocation and interconnection providers is that the switching and interconnection layer aggregating tenant demand functions as an instrument of capital productivity while being priced as transport.

item.title: The cyborg fly: reflexes survive engineered actuators, coordination needs stand-ins
item.description: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.

item.title: A Self-Organizing Swarm Control Model for Underwater Robots Based on Turing-Type Reaction-Diffusion Principles
item.description: In underwater environments, Global Positioning System (GPS) signals and high-speed radio communication are unavailable, and severe constraints exist on communication bandwidth and visibility; consequently, applying conventional swarm formation methods, such as the Boids model, which require the relative positions and velocity vectors of neighboring vehicles, is difficult. This study proposes a decentralized swarm control model that operates without a leader or absolute coordinates, relying solely on the number of received signals from two communication channels with different transmission ranges (inner and outer neighborhoods). The proposed model extends a cellular automaton model based on Turing pattern formation principles to continuous space and is grounded in the fundamental concept that swarms form as robots move toward regions of higher potential calculated from the difference in received signal counts. Specifically, stable behavior is determined through temporal averaging of potential values, hysteresis-based state evaluation, stepwise turning based on temporal differences, and vector composition with an external directional command. Two-dimensional simulation results demonstrated that autonomous swarm formation and control of swarm spatial dispersion via a morphological parameter are achievable, confirming robustness in maintaining swarms and high polarization even under communication dropouts where the communication success rate decreases to approximately 0.7.

item.title: The Self-Assembling Brain: Emergent Routing and Its Open Challenges
item.description: Biologically inspired alternatives to backpropagation, such as feedback alignment, relax the requirement for exact synaptic weight symmetry but still presuppose a fixed, pre-wired correspondence between forward and feedback pathways, an impasse Liao et al. (PNAS, 2026) term "architectural circularity." This commentary examines their Self-Assembling Motif (SAM), which reframes credit assignment as a self-organizing process driven by local synaptic rules. By linking ascending inference and descending feedback streams through initially random cross-stream connections, SAM supports local bridge alignment and emergent pathway alignment during stable training without fixed neuron-to-neuron pairing. Its resulting learning dynamics also exhibit adaptive preconditioning. The commentary highlights the algorithmic, biophysical, and temporal challenges that define the next research frontier: loss of neuron-specific nonlinear gating under straight-through approximation, compounding routing errors in deeper hierarchies, low-dimensional routing bottlenecks, the cortical implementation of non-driving modulatory connections, and the shift from alternating inference-update phases to continuous sensory processing.

item.title: JevBench: Metamorphic Coherence Testing for Typed Probabilistic Decision Models
item.description: Typed probabilistic decision models return distributions over specified answers, such as yes or no, a set of options or levels on an ordered scale. We ask whether their probabilities remain coherent when questions about the same input are reworded, negated, combined, given different options or placed in different batches. JevBench tests this coherence without gold labels. Its 50 metamorphic relations each test one law of probability or choice across five dimensions: representation, batch independence, probability measure, logical order and choice-set conditioning. Each test changes the question or batch while keeping the input fixed. Every model receives the same requests, fixed in advance. JevBench-240 contains 12,000 tests across 240 synthetic cases in 12 decision domains. A fixed subset of 1,200 tests, JevBench-mini, closely reproduces the full-suite ranking (Spearman 0.983). Across 21 openly released models, coherence scores range from 56.5 to 83.9. Batch independence holds for most models. Additivity fails broadly, particularly for complements, where the probabilities of a proposition and its negation should sum to one. A uniform reference model ignores the input and scores 89.4 at chance accuracy, exceeding every evaluated model's coherence score. Among decoders, accuracy ranges from 82.4% to 89.2%, while coherence ranges from 64.2 to 83.9. These results show why both measures are needed to assess decision models. JevBench is available as an open-source Python package.

item.title: How to build and train your recurrent-depth model: A fixed-point perspective
item.description: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.

item.title: Measuring Counterfactual Credit in a Replayable Wildfire-Suppression Benchmark
item.description: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, learned critics are usually evaluated by how well they predict the team's return. Yet predicting a team's return and assigning credit to individual actions are distinct tasks. To test credit directly, we introduce FLARE (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment), a stochastic wildfire suppression benchmark in which any moment of a fire can be replayed with different actions under the same random events. Replaying one step measures the immediate effect of each agent's suppression, which we call simulator credit and use for training. Replaying to the end of the episode measures the effect of each action, which we use for grading critics. In a comparison over eight seeds with multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), simulator credit reduces the interquartile mean burn score (each cell's burning time, capped and averaged over the map; lower is better) from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%. Learned credit from a centralized COMA-style critic does no better than the shared reward. Four trained critics predict the team's return well, yet the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay. The critics also give heterogeneous agents nearly identical action rankings. These results show that a good fit to the team's return is a weak test of a critic's credit.

item.title: Symbolic Proof Compression and Fractal Universality: A Conditional Non-Constructive Refutation of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.description: Building on S.~C.~Woon's (1994) fractal and symbolic reformulation of Voronin's Universality Theorem, we construct a formal, non-constructive proof-by-contradiction architecture exploring the Riemann Hypothesis ($\mathsf{RH}$). Woon's Corollary~3 permits arbitrary finite binary strings to be encoded into nowhere-vanishing exponential waveforms on a closed disk inside the critical strip. Combining effective upper bounds for Voronin universality (Good, Garunkštis) with Cauchy-integral Taylor decoding yields an explicit finite rational grid $\mathcal{G}_{L_0}$ below an effective ceiling $H_{\mathrm{crit}}(L_0)$ within which every formal proof of bit-length at most $L_0$ is imprinted with zero flipped digits. We introduce a conjectural \emph{Zeta-Universal Symbolic Proof Compression Hypothesis} ($\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$), positing that the global regularity implied by $\mathsf{RH}$ compresses true $Π_1^0$ statements about $ζ(s)$ into $\mathsf{ZFC}$ derivations of bounded length $L_0$. Assuming classical logic and $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$, Gödel--Carnap diagonalization over bounded zeta-encoded provability yields a contradiction. The self-referential result converts a digital encoding framework with any uniform proof-compression principle for RH into an immediate non-constructive refutation of RH. Given that, with human input and computer assistance, $\mathsf{RH}$ has been formally verified in the Lean theorem prover strictly within constructive logic, this contradiction does not refute $\mathsf{RH}$. Instead, it falsifies $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$. We conclude by isolating the exact proof-theoretic obstruction---Pudlák's lower bound on bounded reflection proofs---showing why the analytic regularity of $\mathsf{RH}$ cannot compress logical self-reference, and exposing the limits of applying the Law of Excluded Middle to uncomputably bounded searches.

item.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
item.description: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.

item.title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
item.description: We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean~4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.

item.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
item.description: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

item.title: Which Ellipses Are Outlines of a Given Ellipsoid? A Ratio Test with Unknown Focal Length
item.description: When is an image ellipse the outline of a given ellipsoid with semi-axes $a <= b <= c? For a camera with square pixels, zero skew and known principal point, we show that it is an outline at focal length $f$ exactly when a cone ratio kappa(f), computed from two eigenvalues, is at most a/c; the middle semi-axis b plays no role. With f unknown, the admissible focal lengths form an interval; whether it is empty is decided by the smallest cone ratio over $f$, which, when attained, is obtained from an explicit quartic. The interval is bounded above only when the principal point is closer to the long axis of the ellipse than to its short axis. Thus one ellipse can rule out ellipsoids that are too round, never ones that are too elongated, and none if the principal point is unknown. Simulations and 45 Cassini images of Saturn's moons support the test.

item.title: CrossCheck I: Cost Bounds of Imperative Programs as Constrained Optimization, with a Sound Cost Logic and a Verified Certificate Checker
item.description: Static analysis of imperative programs often relies on iterative fixed-point approximations or concrete path exploration. We show that structured imperative control flow---while loops, linear recursion and branching recursion---can be mapped into constrained optimization problems over the free monoid of execution traces and the free algebra of computation trees. Ordering traces and trees by an intensional \textit{order-by-composition} ($\sqsubseteq$), halting is characterized as finding the minimal trace or tree that satisfies the exit condition, and we prove that this characterization coincides with the standard big-step semantics. Exact state recurrences are undecidable in general, so we relax them into cost envelopes, using ranking potentials and the tropical $(\max,+)$ reading of the timing schema, and obtain sound upper bounds on execution cost. The bounds compose over whole programs in a cost logic for a small language with nondeterministic actions, procedures, recursion and assumed contracts, which we prove sound for terminating and non-terminating executions. A linear instance of the logic has certificates---programs annotated with invariants, potentials and Farkas multipliers---and a checker that validates them with integer arithmetic only; an accepted certificate bounds the cost of every execution. All results, the checker and the worked examples are machine-checked in Lean~4. A companion paper describes a Clang plugin that produces such certificates and its evaluation.

item.title: Two messages suffice for quantum interactive proof systems
item.description: Quantum interactive proof systems can be parallelized to three messages, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), perhaps their most striking distinction from classical counterparts. In this work, we establish that any quantum interactive proof system can further be parallelized to two messages, with the verifier sending halves of EPR pairs (``quantum public coins'') and, after the prover's response, using only stoquastic verification. Technically, we strengthen ${\sf QIP}(3) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}$ of Jain, Ji, Upadhyay, and Watrous (JACM, 2011) and fully characterize two-message quantum interactive proof systems by proving \[ {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf StoqAM} = {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM} = {\sf QIP}(2) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}. \] Our main technical contributions show that Close Image to Uniform (CIUniform), which is naturally in the stoquastic version of ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$, is $\sf PSPACE$-hard via transforming the sum-check protocol of Shamir (JACM, 1992) and Shen (JACM, 1992) into a CIUniform instance consisting of an efficient sampler whose image distribution is exactly uniform for some input distribution when the underlying quantified Boolean formula is true.

item.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
item.description: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

item.title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
item.description: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

item.title: Cop-Win Edge Completion: Hardness, Structure, and Parameterized Algorithm
item.description: We study Cop-Win Edge Completion: given a graph $G$, find the minimum number $\copfill(G)$ of edges whose addition lets one cop capture a visible robber. We first give an exact reduction from Dominating Set, constructing for every nonempty graph $H$ a graph $G_H$ on $2|V(H)|+2$ vertices with $\copfill(G_H)=γ(H)$. This resolves a complexity question of Mertzios et al. and implies NP-completeness even for connected graphs of diameter two with a dominating edge and domination number two. Interestingly, while Minimum Fill-in is fixed-parameter tractable in the number $k$ of added edges, Cop-Win Edge Completion, whose target class strictly contains the connected chordal graphs, is W[2]-hard parameterized by $k$, even by $k+γ(G)$. We then give two lower bounds. The first, $\copfill(G)\ge 2n-m-b-c-1$, where $n,m,b,c$ count vertices, edges, nontrivial blocks, and components, is tight for partial 2-trees, giving a linear-time algorithm for the optimum value and a quadratic-time construction; for outerplanar graphs, an optimum completion preserving outerplanarity is found in linear time. The second, based on the cycle space modulo the subspace generated by triangles, gives $\copfill(G)=c-1+\sum_{i=1}^r(\ell_i-3)$ for block-cactus graphs with long cycle blocks of lengths $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r$. We also show how the optimum behaves under disjoint unions and joins, yielding a polynomial-time algorithm for $P_4$-sparse graphs, including cographs, and exact formulas for complete multipartite graphs. In contrast to partial 2-trees and block-cactus graphs, an optimum cop-win completion can be much smaller than a minimum chordal one, already on complete bipartite graphs. Finally, we give FPT algorithms for $k+\mathrm{nd}(G)$, for the twin-cover number $t$ alone in time $2^{O(t^3)}n^{O(1)}$, and for $k+\mathrm{tw}(G)$.

item.title: So Many Ways to Multiply $3\times3$ Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
item.description: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). The dataset shows that the number of different rank patterns is much larger than previously known.

item.title: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games
item.description: We study learning in two-player zero-sum games, also known as matrix games, in which two players with $m$ and $n$ actions repeatedly select mixed strategies for $T$ rounds. The learning dynamics based on optimistic Hedge guarantee regrets of $O(\log(mn))$, which improve to $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ if each player knows the number of actions of the opponent, whereas matching regret lower bounds have been known only for specific learning dynamics. We prove that, for every deterministic learning dynamic, there exists a payoff matrix for which the maximum individual regret is $Ω(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ for a wide range of $m$ and $n$. Together with the upper bound $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$, this lower bound shows that the minimax regret of deterministic learning dynamics in matrix games is $Θ(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ in this regime. For all $m$, $n$, and $T$, we also prove the lower bound $Ω(\min\{T,\log\min\{m,n\}\})$. These lower bounds hold even if each player also observes the strategies and the feedback of the opponent. Our main technical contribution is an adaptive construction of the payoff matrix. While running the algorithms of the two players, we add in each round a rank-one matrix that keeps the feedback of the previous rounds unchanged and increases a lower bound on the sum of the regrets of the two players. As by-products, we obtain lower bounds on the rate at which the average strategies converge to a Nash equilibrium and on the query complexity of matrix-vector products that deterministic algorithms need to compute an approximate Nash equilibrium.

item.title: Approximate Minimum Triangle Partitions
item.description: Let $ρ(P)$ be the minimum number of triangles in a partition of a simple polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices where triangle corners may be arbitrary points (Steiner points). It is not known whether $ρ(P)$ can be computed in polynomial time. We do not assume general position: when vertices of $P$ are collinear, a triangle side may pass through several vertices, and good partitions exploit this. Every vertex of $P$ is a corner of some triangle of every partition, so $ρ(P) \ge n/3$, and any triangulation, with $n-2$ triangles, is a 3-approximation that can be computed in $O(n)$ time. This is the best factor known. We improve it in two steps. First, let $ρ_0(P)$ be the minimum number of triangles over partitions whose corners are all vertices of $P$, which can be computed in $O(n^3)$ time (Asano, Asano, and Pinter, 1986). We prove that $ρ_0(P) \le 2ρ(P)-2$ unless $P$ is a triangle, which is tight. Thus Steiner points save at most half of the triangles and $ρ_0(P)$ is a 2-approximation, computed in $O(n^3)$ time. Second, we break the factor-2 barrier of Steiner-free partitions. We observe that $ρ_0(P)$ is close to $2ρ(P)$ only if optimal partitions have few Steiner points, each with many triangles around it. We handle this case by a dynamic program over partitions in which every Steiner point in the interior of $P$ is joined to a vertex of $P$ by a straight run of triangle sides, giving a 5/3-approximation in $O(n^{12})$ time.

item.title: SRCWDNet: Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network for Multi-Label Remote Sensing Scene Classification
item.description: Multi-label remote sensing scene classification remains a challenging task due to complex spatial-spectral patterns, extreme class imbalance, and inter-label dependencies that are often insufficiently modeled. To address these challenges, we introduce a Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network (SRCWDNet), which integrates three key modules: (1) a Cross-Window Attention module that captures local and global visual context through learnable global tokens; (2) a Dual Label-Graph module that adaptively combines statistical co-occurrence graphs and learned semantic-embedding graphs to facilitate label-relational reasoning; and (3) a Neural Classifier Chain that sequentially predicts labels to exploit inter-label dependencies. Evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and trained with an Asymmetric-Graph-Consistency loss, SRCWDNet achieves accuracies of 98.93% and 96.53%, with corresponding F1-scores of 0.9365 and 0.8723 on the MLRSNet and China-MAS50k datasets, respectively, outperforming CNN, transformer, and lightweight baselines. These findings demonstrate that jointly modeling visual attention and adaptive label correlations can substantially improve multi-label remote sensing scene classification, particularly under long-tailed class distributions.

item.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
item.description: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

item.title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
item.description: Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(DΦ) = 1) without topological folding (det(DΦ) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox). We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(Ω) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(Ω). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations). We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(DΦ)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.

item.title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
item.description: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

item.title: Planar Graphs Embed into Graphs with Treewidth $O(\log n /ε)$
item.description: We construct a stochastic embedding of $n$-vertex planar graphs into graphs of treewidth $O(\log n/ε)$ and expected distortion $1+ε$ for any parameter $ε\in (0,1)$. This result yields randomized polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTASes) for a broad class of connectivity problems on planar graphs, including the $k$-MST problem. The treewidth bound is asymptotically optimal and settles a conjecture of Chang, Cohen-Addad, Conroy, Le, Ma. Pilipczuk, and Mi. Pilipczuk (2025). The key idea is a new construction of a stochastic balanced cut of size $O(\log n/ε)$ and expected distortion $1+ε/\log n$ for every edge. We construct these cuts using the minimax principle, an approach that differs significantly from existing cut constructions based on a random clustering hierarchy. Our embedding extends to minor-free graphs using the Robertson-Seymour decomposition, giving the same treewidth bound. Using this decomposition, we obtain the first randomized PTASes for many connectivity problems in minor-free graphs, including the Steiner tree problem and its prize-collecting variant.

item.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests
item.description: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

item.title: What Do Sound Event Embeddings Reveal? Auditing Speaker Leakage in Audio Representations
item.description: Pretrained audio embeddings are increasingly used as intermediate representations for sound event detection (SED) and other always-on acoustic sensing tasks. While these representations are selected for their utility on downstream tasks, they may also retain sensitive information unrelated to their intended purpose, creating privacy risks even when raw audio is not exposed. In this work, we present an empirical framework for auditing privacy leakage from pretrained audio embeddings using two complementary approaches. First, we quantify representation-level leakage by measuring statistical dependence between an audio embedding and a representation specialized for encoding sensitive information. Second, we measure attack-level leakage by training lightweight adversarial probes to recover sensitive attributes directly from the embedding. We apply this framework to four widely used audio representations (CLAP, PANNs, AST, and YAMNet) and evaluate leakage of speaker identity and gender. We found that speaker identification balanced accuracy ranges from $0.43$ to $0.72$, while gender information is also strongly recoverable. Moreover, representation-level and attack-based measurements exhibit consistent trends, with CLAP leaking the most and YAMNet leaking the lest speaker identity. These results demonstrate that intermediate audio representations are not inherently privacy-preserving interfaces and motivate privacy leakage as an explicit criterion, alongside downstream utility, when selecting representations for acoustic sensing systems.

item.title: Déjà VAE: When Do Autoencoder Traces Reveal Generated Images?
item.description: A latent diffusion model's output has already passed through its autoencoder, so a second round trip changes it very little. This "déjà vu" underlies reconstruction-based detectors of generated images; we analyse when it reveals a generated image and when it does not. Read by a frozen vision foundation model without training, the trace is strongest in intermediate layers, and, unlike pixel-level reconstruction error, it treats blur as a sign of a real image. It belongs to the generator's exact decoder: on Synthbuster, the exact decoders of Stable Diffusion 1.3, 1.4, 2 and XL are the strongest of eight autoencoders and catch 94-100% of their generators' images at a 5% false-alarm rate (SDXL's version identified post hoc), while near-identical versions catch 7-42%. A detector trained only on real photographs and their autoencoder copies matches one trained on 162k generated images on GenImage (+2.3 points, 95% CI [0.9, 3.7]) and complements it in fusion, but one resize with JPEG re-save, or a mild blur, costs it 19-27 points. Two lessons concern benchmarks. The in-the-wild benchmark Chameleon can be solved from image width alone. And on Synthbuster, how the real photographs are matched to the generated images' size decides whether our detector leads or trails (+4.4 or -9.7 points): the matching protocol alone can reverse a detector comparison. Code and per-image scores: https://github.com/iamsaugatpandey/deja-vae

item.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
item.description: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.

item.title: DiffSimp: Differentiable Mesh Simplification for Gradient-Based Low-Poly Modeling
item.description: Differentiable mesh extraction enables gradient-based optimization of detailed 3D geometry across diverse tasks. However, compact meshes are commonly obtained through post-processing simplification, leaving simplification-induced errors outside upstream optimization. We introduce DiffSimp, a training-free, drop-in differentiable mesh simplification layer built on QEM-based parallel edge collapse, enabling existing geometry optimization pipelines to optimize their final simplified meshes. We formulate simplification under a fixed collapse history as a locally differentiable collapse map, enabling gradient propagation without relaxing discrete collapse decisions. We combine fast, high-quality parallel simplification with a factorized backward formulation that exploits differentiable vertex quadrics and quadric reduction forests for efficient gradient propagation. Experiments on low-poly mesh reconstruction and inverse rendering demonstrate improved fidelity over post-processing simplification, with additional gains from gradient propagation that increase under tighter vertex budgets. DiffSimp supports diverse geometry optimization frontends, with 1.00-1.25$\times$ the end-to-end runtime of unsimplified baselines in evaluated pipelines.

item.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
item.description: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the \emph{trainable policy} velocity onto rollouts from a \emph{behavior distribution}. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This \emph{behavior--policy mismatch} breaks baseline invariance and injects \emph{baseline-induced gradient drift}, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose \textbf{I}nstantaneous \textbf{T}rajectory \textbf{D}istribution \textbf{M}atching (\textbf{iTDM}), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly $3\times$ faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to $0.87$ without collapse. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

item.title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
item.description: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

item.title: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining
item.description: A language model played three representatives, each instructed to get the best payoff for its own group. One representative requested a plan, another chose the sole offer, and all three voted. If anyone voted no, each group received its fallback payoff. In 60 games with Qwen3-Next-80B, the representative at risk of a loss always requested a plan that would leave everyone better off. In each game, two copies of the proposer saw the same payoffs, peer request and reminder that the offer needed three yes votes. Showing the proposer how many groups gained under each plan raised mutually beneficial agreements from 6/60 to 31/60 (paired increase 41.7 percentage points, conservative 95% interval 18.8 to 58.5). Two of the four plans benefited everyone, so picking uniformly would put a mutual gain on the ballot half the time on average. In an earlier study, GPT-4.1 played 12 conflict games under two message conditions. Majority rule passed 15 of 24 offers, all at one group's expense. Unanimity passed two, both mutual gains. In the Qwen games, voters never saw the counts. They approved all 37 offers that helped everyone. On all 83 offers that would have cost one group points, its representative voted no.

item.title: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
item.description: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $π_v/β_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(π_v/β_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

item.title: LimeTree: Linear-Memory Graph Neural Networks over Tree-Graphs for Resource-Efficient Language Modeling and Context Extrapolation
item.description: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 13 in 35 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

item.title: Closed-Form Formula for $d_{\mathrm{critical}}(a_0)$ in Large Fully Connected Power Grids
item.description: Kadloor and Santhi (arXiv:1011.4098) modeled cascading failures in a large fully connected power grid by a coupled four-variable recursion for the minimum surviving load $a_n$, the mean failed load $μ_{n-1}$, the redistributed load $\mathcal{D}_n$, and the stagewise failure probability $p_n$. They noted that the recursion was not tractable and identified the critical disturbance $d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ by simulation. We show that the recursion telescopes exactly into a one-dimensional monotone map $a_{n+1} = g(a_n)$. This yields the threshold in closed form: $1 - a_0 = d_{\mathrm{critical}}\,(1 + \ln(1 + 1/d_{\mathrm{critical}}))$, or explicitly in terms of the lower branch $W_{-1}$ of the Lambert W function. We prove a sharp dichotomy. For $d_m \le d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ the cascade halts with limiting load $a_0 + d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ at criticality and surviving fraction $1/(1 + d_{\mathrm{critical}})$. For $d_m > d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ a complete outage occurs in finitely many steps.

item.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
item.description: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

item.title: CableMoE: Harm-Regularized Mean-Residual Expert Fusion for Transmission-Corridor Segmentation
item.description: Semantic mapping of transmission corridors benefits from heterogeneous LiDAR and image-guided predictors, but replacing a strong ensemble with a learned router can damage rare electrical assets. We introduce CableMoE, a post-hoc mixture of four frozen segmentation experts.
